findings.section: Relevance; also KC2 (16, incl. concept anchor), Questions 55, WTLF 113, When-to-Use 132, Worked Example 149, Anti-patterns 156
findings.claim: Carroll's four-component CSR pyramid for ethics decisions affecting users (Ch 2.3)

findings.evidence: Deep 879: 'Pyramid of corporate social responsibility ... presented in source without a theorist attribution (Ch 2.3) [AP]'. Converted source: the only 'Carroll' is a reporter byline in the endnotes (50299).
findings.fix: correct: replace 'Carroll's (four-component CSR) pyramid' with 'the four-component CSR pyramid' at 8, 16, 55, 113, 132, 149, 156; change the line-16 anchor to `<!-- concept: corporate-social-responsibility -->` (the slug the decision-making distillation uses).

findings.claim: the operations chapter (Ch 10) is the corpus's only structured treatment of the make-or-buy decision as a procurement primitive
findings.failure_mode: OpenStax Accounting Vol 2 carries a structured make-or-buy analysis (avoidable-cost comparison with a worked example). The distillation's own Integration row (line 172) says so.
findings.evidence: openstax-accounting-vol2-deep 17, 279-281 ('Make-or-buy decisions ... compares the avoidable cost of producing internally to the cost of purchasing externally').
findings.fix: correct: the operations chapter (Ch 10.4) gives the qualitative make-or-buy criteria (quantity, secrecy, supplier reliability and quality); OpenStax Accounting Vol 2 (Ch 10.3) gives the relevant-cost arithmetic.

findings.section: Software-Business Relevance; also Questions 88, Named Limits 185

findings.failure_mode: VPN and ASP are in the converted source's Ch 13 but not in the deep ref, which lists networks (LAN, WAN, internet, intranets, extranets), MIS, technology planning, protection and trends. The deep ref places ERP under Ch 10.4.

Other names for ASPs include on-demand software, hosted applications, and software-as-a-service') (Ch 13.2).

findings.claim: For a software company, the irresponsible-but-legal category is where most data-handling, AI-deployment, and dark-pattern decisions sit.
findings.failure_mode: An empirical claim ('most') with no basis in the source or deep ref, sitting under a source citation.
findings.evidence: Deep 91: the three categories, with legal-and-responsible 'the vast majority'; nothing on software or data handling.
findings.fix: correct: For a software company, data-handling, AI-deployment and dark-pattern decisions are candidates for the irresponsible-but-legal category and should be tested against it.

findings.claim: Each group has distinct engagement modalities and indicators of trust.
findings.failure_mode: The source sets out the business's distinct responsibilities to each group; 'engagement modalities' and 'indicators of trust' are not in it.
findings.evidence: Deep 95-100: responsibilities to employees, customers, society, investors.
findings.fix: correct: The source sets out the business's distinct responsibilities to each group (jobs and a safe, fair workplace; delivering what is promised; jobs, taxes and environmental care; economic return).

findings.section: Key Concepts 7 (Gantt, CPM, PERT); also Questions 66
findings.claim: the CPM-vs-PERT choice turns on whether the activity-time variance is large enough to warrant the three-estimate discipline
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the converted source (CPM assumes task times are known with certainty; PERT's three estimates handle uncertainty) but not carried by the deep ref.
findings.evidence: Source 27554-27560: 'CPM assumes that the amount of time needed to finish a task is known with certainty ... In contrast, PERT assigns three time estimates for each activity'. Deep 463 lacks the certainty contrast.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 463 'CPM assumes that the amount of time needed to finish a task is known with certainty; therefore, the CPM diagram shows only one number for the time needed to complete each activity' (Ch 10.5).

findings.claim: Risk-return trade-off as universal financial principle. ... The principle extends beyond financial management to any software-business decision where loss probability and gain magnitude can be characterised ... (Source: Ch 16.1)
findings.failure_mode: The source calls it 'a basic principle in finance' and 'widely accepted', not universal, and applies it to financial managers' investment and financing decisions. The extension beyond finance is the distillation's own but is cited to Ch 16.1.
findings.fix: correct: **Risk-return trade-off.** 'A basic principle in finance' (Ch 16.1): "The higher the risk, the greater the return that is required" [V]. ... Applied here (the distillation's extension, not the source's) to feature investment, reliability spend, security hardening and technical-debt remediation.

findings.claim: Four primary sources ... (Source: App A, "Contract Law")
findings.failure_mode: Mis-cited section: the four sources of law are in 'The Main Sources of Law'; only the contract elements come from 'Contract Law'.
findings.evidence: Deep 779 (App A, 'The Main Sources of Law'), 787 (App A, 'Contract Law').
findings.fix: correct: (Source: App A, "The Main Sources of Law"; "Contract Law")

findings.claim: For a software-business, the copyright regime governs source code by default; the patent regime governs software-implemented inventions (with jurisdictional variation) ... (97: copyright (life-plus-70 for printed/digital work))
findings.failure_mode: The source's copyright covers printed materials, works of art, photographs and movies; it says nothing about software or digital works. The software mappings are the distillation's legal extension, presented under the source citation.
findings.fix: correct: mark the software mapping as the distillation's application ('Applied to software (not in the source): ...'); at 97 replace 'printed/digital work' with 'printed materials, art, photographs, movies'.

findings.section: Key Concepts 15 (Strict product liability); also WTLF 120, When-to-Use 129, Worked Example 149, Anti-patterns 162
findings.claim: For software, strict-liability exposure rises in regulated domains (medical, financial, transport) and is a load-bearing consideration for any product-launch decision touching consumer safety.
findings.failure_mode: The source never applies strict liability to software. Its doctrine covers personal injury or property damage from defective products or packaging; whether and how it reaches software is a legal premise the source does not supply. The same premise carries the What-to-Look-For pattern, a When-to-Use gate, a worked-example step and an anti-pattern.
findings.evidence: Deep 799. Source 49661-49665: 'A manufacturer or seller is liable for any personal injury or property damage caused by defective products or packaging—even if all possible care was used'.
findings.fix: correct: The source's strict-liability doctrine covers personal injury or property damage caused by defective products, even if all possible care was taken (App A). Whether it reaches a software product is a question for OpenStax Business Law or counsel; this source does not address software.

findings.claim: Five-step decision-making process for non-programmed decisions.
findings.failure_mode: The source says managers follow the five steps whether a decision is programmed or non-programmed.
findings.evidence: Deep 250; source 16451: 'Whether a decision is programmed or nonprogrammed, managers typically follow five steps in the decision making process'.
findings.fix: correct: **Five-step decision-making process** (for programmed and non-programmed decisions alike).

findings.claim: Most large organisations combine
findings.failure_mode: Quantifier raised: the source says 'many'.
findings.evidence: Deep 278; source 18144: 'Many large organizations use several types of departmentalization.'
findings.fix: correct: Many large organisations combine several types

findings.claim: Are workers underperforming because hygiene factors (policy, supervision, working conditions) are absent (Herzberg)?
findings.failure_mode: Inverts the source's account of Herzberg. Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but 'could not serve as a source of satisfaction or motivation'; good working conditions 'won't make them work harder'. For performance the source points to motivating factors (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility); lacking them, workers do 'an adequate job, rather than their best'. The question omits motivators.
findings.fix: correct: Are workers doing adequate rather than best work because motivating factors (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility) are missing (Herzberg)? Are they dissatisfied or leaving because hygiene factors (policy, supervision, working conditions) are poor?

findings.claim: The collapse is the most common ethics failure mode.
findings.failure_mode: Frequency claim with no basis in the source or deep ref.
findings.evidence: Deep 89-91: pyramid and three categories; no frequency data.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Is this a product whose defect could cause physical or financial harm to users? Strict liability applies even when all possible care was taken
findings.failure_mode: Widens the doctrine: the source's strict liability covers personal injury or property damage, not financial harm. (The software premise is covered by the line-42 finding.)
findings.fix: correct: Is this a product whose defect could cause personal injury or property damage? Under strict liability (App A) the manufacturer or seller is liable even when all possible care was taken.

findings.claim: Autocratic in crisis with clear authority; participative when the team is mature; free-rein when expectations are clear and feedback channels work.
findings.failure_mode: 'Autocratic in crisis' is not the source's case for the autocratic style; it gives the military ('by necessity') and newly hired employees who have not yet learned the job. Participative or free-rein then suits 'established' employees; free-rein works with highly motivated, experienced personnel.
findings.evidence: Deep 228-232. Source 15948-15951 (military), 16150-16159 (situational leadership: new hires respond to authoritative leadership until established), 16031 table (free-rein works well with highly motivated, experienced, educated personnel).
findings.fix: correct: Authoritative for people still learning the job; participative or free-rein once they are established; free-rein only when expectations are clear and feedback flows (Ch 6.4).

findings.claim: Inconsistent multi-channel messaging is the standard stakeholder-confusion source.
findings.failure_mode: The source says disjointed promotion led many companies to adopt IMC; 'the standard stakeholder-confusion source' is an unsupported generalisation.
findings.evidence: Source 34142-34146: 'This disjointed approach to promotion has propelled many companies to adopt the concept of integrated marketing communications (IMC).' Deep 588.
findings.fix: correct: The source presents IMC as the answer to disjointed promotion, which led many companies to adopt it (Ch 12.5).

findings.claim: PERT assigns "three time estimates per activity (optimistic, most probable, pessimistic) to anticipate delays." (Source: Ch 10.5, "Scheduling")

findings.claim: The seven-environment wheel, make-or-buy criteria, CPM/PERT distinction, MRP/MRP-II/ERP hierarchy, TQM/DMAIC framing, four-ratio category structure, strict-liability doctrine, and Carroll's pyramid are all [AP] in the deep reference
findings.failure_mode: Only the seven sub-environments (deep 35) and the pyramid (deep 879) carry [AP]; make-or-buy, CPM/PERT, MRP/ERP, ratios and strict liability are unmarked in the deep ref, and TQM's continuous-improvement definition is [V]. 'Carroll's' repeats the misattribution.
findings.fix: correct: The seven-environment wheel and the CSR pyramid are [AP] in the deep reference; the make-or-buy, CPM/PERT, MRP/ERP, ratio and strict-liability material is unmarked paraphrase there, and the continuous-improvement definition is [V].

notes: Most serious: (1) the Carroll misattribution runs through seven lines and a concept anchor, and the citation notes claim the deep ref attributes the pyramid to 'Carroll (1991)', which the deep ref explicitly denies; (2) the Herzberg question inverts the source (hygiene factors do not drive performance); (3) the five-step process is again restricted to non-programmed decisions; (4) 'the corpus's only structured treatment of make-or-buy' is contradicted by Accounting Vol 2 and by this distillation's own line 172. Software applications of strict liability and copyright are the distillation's legal extensions and are not flagged as such. Integration rows were checked against each sibling deep ref: principles-marketing, accounting-vol2, business-law, entrepreneurship and principles-finance rows hold; PoM, Business Ethics, OB, Jones and Letaw rows each carry one or two items the sibling deep ref lacks, and the Jones and Letaw rows are stale ('pending ingest'). [V] quotations checked against the converted source: 'generally beyond the control of management and change constantly' (1536), 'adapters' (1568), continuous improvement (27631), 'higher the risk' (44274), promotion definition (33930), 'get stuck at any stage' (16470), Six Sigma 3.4 (27654) all exact; the Ch 1.2 quote at 141 is elided without an ellipsis. The auditing definition at line 36 is exact but comes from the Ch 14 Key Terms glossary (source 40692-40702), not Ch 14.2 'Public Accountants': the deep ref (619) carries the same mis-cite, and Key Terms is a section the deep ref's coverage note excludes. Deep-ref marker note: the Brigham Young classification (deep 77) is marked [AP], but the source relays BYU researchers ('Researchers from Brigham Young University tell us', source 4897), so [BT] fits better; the distillation's [BT] at 183 is the better marker. The worked example's figures (22% of ARR, six months, three-year SLA) are scenario-internal. Claim count is approximate (about 158 discrete claims); grouped findings cover repeated lines as listed in each finding's section field.
